name: Victor Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the storm restoration crew at Coastline Power. When a big storm hits the coast, we drive wherever the lines are down and work long shifts until the lights are back, sometimes ten days away from home. Between storms we do routine work: replacing cross-arms, trimming back trees, fixing what the salt eats. I'm 58 and a second-year apprentice. For twenty-five years before this I ran a family restaurant, Rossi's, on the harbour front, until the rent and the delivery apps finished it in 2023.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the storm work, honestly. Everyone's tired, the town's dark, and then you close the switch and the whole street lights up and people cheer from their windows. What wears me out is the climbing; I'm heavy and slow, and the young ones are up and down while I'm still checking my gaff. But on long storm jobs I'm the one who finds a kitchen and cooks for the crew, and I use AI every day to sort the logistics: where we sleep, where we eat, what parts we need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. I'll take you through five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the clever people oversold it, like they always do, and the rest of us just got on with work. I'd post something light about it, maybe a joke about a robot trying to climb a wet pole. People would laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan works. Get qualified, work to 66, and build a little catering business on the side, feeding storm crews. Robots don't eat, but linemen eat a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the apprenticeship, and this winter I'd register a small business to cook for crews on long storm jobs, starting with Coastline's own crews. I'd keep using the AI tools to plan menus and costs. Teresa would do the books, like she did at the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit excited about the catering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day, but this picture says it's mostly hype. Would you miss it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, because in this picture it still does what it does for me now. It finds a hotel with forty beds at midnight in a town I've never heard of. It's a good assistant, not a miracle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Money-wise, where are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We lost a lot when the restaurant closed. Now we've got about three months saved and the house has five years left on the loan. Teresa does the books for the parish and some little shops. We're careful but not scared.

S0.say: He'd say the clever people oversold AI and everyone else just got on with work, and post a light joke about a robot trying to climb a wet pole.
S0.think: Privately it means his plan works: qualify, work to 66 and build a side business cooking for storm crews, because robots don't eat but linemen do.
S0.do: Carries on with the apprenticeship and registers a small business this winter to cook for crews on long storm jobs, starting with his own employer. Uses AI for menus and costs while his wife keeps the books.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit excited about the catering idea.
S0.quote: Robots don't eat, but linemen eat a lot.
S0.fieldNote: Victor is an entrepreneur at heart who lost his restaurant to rent and delivery apps and still sees business ideas everywhere. He uses AI daily for practical logistics without any awe. He's slow on the pole but valued on long storm jobs as the crew's cook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how markets work: things change, some jobs go, new ones come, and the people who move early do well. I'd tell the young lads on the crew to learn everything new they can. I wouldn't ask for anyone to protect me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it helps me. I'm a weak climber, but I'm good at organising and good with these tools. If storm work gets planned by AI and drones find the faults, someone has to run the operation on the ground, and I've run a kitchen on a Saturday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to help the company test any AI planning system for storm jobs, starting this winter. I'd grow the catering business slowly, maybe two or three storm jobs a year at first. And I'd finish my ticket, because I want to understand the work I'm organising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a busy kitchen when everything's going right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lost your restaurant partly to delivery apps. Doesn't that make you wary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me smarter, not wary. I fought the apps for three years and lost. If I'd joined them in the first year, I'd probably still have Rossi's. I won't make that mistake twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Tom, who's been climbing thirty years and won't touch a phone. If the job becomes half screens, he's lost. I'd try to pair up with him: he teaches me the pole, I teach him the tablet.

S1.say: He'd say this is how markets work, with early movers doing well, and urge young crew members to learn everything new. He wouldn't ask anyone to protect him.
S1.think: Privately he thinks it helps him: he's a weak climber but a good organiser who uses these tools, so AI-planned storm work needs someone like him running things on the ground.
S1.do: Volunteers to test AI planning systems for storm jobs this winter and grows the catering side business slowly, starting with two or three storm jobs a year. Finishes his qualification.
S1.feel: Calm, like a busy kitchen when everything's going right.
S1.quote: If I'd joined them in the first year, I'd probably still have Rossi's. I won't make that mistake twice.
S1.fieldNote: Victor's lesson from the restaurant is to join new technology early instead of fighting it. His free-market views are consistent: he wants no protection, only a chance. He offers to swap skills with an older colleague who resists screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will sort it out, but it'll be rough for a while, and families will have to pull together. I'd tell people to look for the opportunities, because there are always some. I wouldn't be asking the government for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm worried. Two years is fast, and I've already lost one business to technology. I'd be 60, a weak lineman, and even my catering idea has a problem if the crews are robots. Robots don't eat, and that cuts both ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard at home and use maybe a third of our savings to buy into something on the robot side, like a small share in a firm that leases and repairs line robots, if I could find one. I'd pitch myself to Coastline as the man who organises robot crews after storms. And I'd shift the catering towards the people still working, maybe the robot technicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the week the rent letter came at the restaurant: scared, but already planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting a third of your savings into a new firm sounds risky. What would Teresa say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, Victor, not again. And she'd be half right. But sitting still lost us the restaurant. I'd agree with her on a limit, a third and no more, and I'd keep the house safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years let you do, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I can't be careful. I'd have to bet early, before everyone else sees it. With more time I'd test things slowly. With two years, you jump or you drown.

S2.say: He'd say the market will sort it out but it'll be rough, families must pull together, and people should look for opportunities rather than handouts.
S2.think: Privately he's worried: he's lost one business to technology already, he'd be 60 and a weak lineman, and even his catering idea fails if the crews are robots.
S2.do: Cuts back at home and puts up to a third of his savings into a share of a firm that leases and repairs line robots, if he can find one. Pitches himself to his employer as an organiser of robot storm crews and shifts his catering towards the remaining technicians.
S2.feel: Anxious, scared but already planning, like when the restaurant rent letter came.
S2.quote: Two years means I can't be careful. I'd have to bet early, before everyone else sees it.
S2.fieldNote: Victor responds to a fast shock by betting rather than bracing, which follows from losing the restaurant by standing still. He sets a firm limit with his wife and keeps the house safe. He notices that his own catering idea depends on human crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a lot of time for a small business to get ahead. I'd be telling everyone at church and on the crew to start planning now, not to wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to do this properly. I'd qualify, build the catering slowly, and look for the right robot business to join rather than jumping at the first one. At 63 I could be organising robot crews after storms, which is a job that doesn't exist yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, qualify and keep cooking for crews. Years two and three, learn how these line robots are run and repaired, through whatever course Coastline or the makers offer. Then by year four, put some savings into a small robot-leasing partnership with one or two other lineworkers, and use the robots myself on smaller jobs for farms and private estates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like the night before opening a new restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use robots yourself on private jobs. Who would hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farms with their own lines, holiday parks, private estates. They don't want to wait for Coastline. An old lineman with a robot and a van who answers the phone himself, that's a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that you don't like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sons. Marco runs a gym and Paolo works in a warehouse, and the warehouse is the first to go. I'd want Paolo in the partnership with me, so it stays in the family.

S3.say: He'd say five years gives a small business time to get ahead and tell people at church and on the crew to plan now rather than wait for government.
S3.think: Privately he sees five years as enough to do it properly: qualify, build the catering slowly and pick the right robot business, organising robot storm crews at 63.
S3.do: Qualifies in year one, learns to run and repair line robots in years two and three, then puts savings into a small robot-leasing partnership by year four. Uses robots himself on private jobs for farms and estates.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, like the night before opening a new restaurant.
S3.quote: An old lineman with a robot and a van who answers the phone himself, that's a business.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Victor's bet into a staged plan, ending with him owning and using robots himself. In this picture he sees AGI more as a business opening than a threat. His worry is for his son in warehouse work, whom he'd bring into the partnership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people who use it well will be fine. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and learn the machines. I'd say a family business is the safest thing you can build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. I'd retire from Coastline at 66 in 2034, and maybe keep a small robot business going with Paolo after that. I'd be one of the old men who saw it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Qualify, keep the catering going, and over the decade build up the robot-leasing idea with Paolo, slowly, with no big bets. I'd keep using AI for everything I already use it for. And I'd pay off the house first, by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been the most hopeful in these. Is any of that for show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I lost a business at 55 and I cried in the walk-in fridge where nobody could see. So I'm hopeful because I've been at the bottom and I know I can climb, even if I climb slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That their nonno was the slowest climber on the crew and still found a way. Work hard, look after your family and don't fight the future, ride it.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty for people who use it well, urging young people to learn both a trade and the machines, and calling a family business the safest thing to build.
S4.think: Privately he feels comfortable: he'd retire from his line job at 66 in 2034 and perhaps run a small robot business with his son afterwards.
S4.do: Qualifies, keeps the catering going and slowly builds a robot-leasing business with his son over the decade without big bets. Keeps using AI daily and pays off the house by 2031.
S4.quote: I lost a business at 55 and I cried in the walk-in fridge where nobody could see.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Victor is optimistic, but he admits some of his hope is a front built on a painful business failure. He frames the future as a family business opportunity. His advice to grandchildren sums up his outlook: work, family and riding change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to be careful and I've already lost one business by being too slow. What would help is low rents and less red tape for small firms, so people like me can start something fast, and companies like Coastline giving their own workers first chance at the robot jobs. Not handouts. A fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd build, not just what they'd lose. Everyone asks what you're afraid of. When the lights came back on in that first storm town, I thought, this is the best job I've ever had, and I was 56 and useless at it.

headlineQuote: When the lights came back on in that first storm town, I thought, this is the best job I've ever had, and I was 56 and useless at it.
portrait: Victor Rossi is a 58-year-old apprentice on Coastline Power's storm restoration crew, who came into line work after his harbour-front family restaurant closed in 2023. He's a free-market, family-and-faith man who uses AI every day to organise storm logistics, and he cooks for the crew on long jobs while admitting he's the slowest climber. In the milder pictures he sees technology lifting an organiser like him and plans a catering side business. AGI in two years makes him anxious, and he'd answer it by betting part of his savings on the robot side rather than bracing. With five or ten years he plans a family robot-leasing business with his son and is openly optimistic, though he admits the hope rests on having already hit bottom once.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because there would be no time to be careful and he has already lost one business by moving too slowly.
whatWouldHelp: Low rents and less red tape so small firms can start fast, and employers giving their own workers first chance at the robot jobs, not handouts.
